guide.title: Read this as a consistency design first, and a peak-traffic story second.
guide.problem: Inventory changes arrived from checkout and warehouse operations at the same time. During major sales, database locking protected correctness but limited throughput; relaxing consistency kept the site alive but created overselling and cancelled orders.
guide.core_idea: Put every mutation through one ordered command log, rebuild in-memory state from queue offsets, process conflicts on a single thread and persist changes asynchronously in batches. Integrations use reserve, confirm and reverse instead of pretending that several HTTP services share one atomic transaction.
guide.outcome: The article reports roughly 350k in-memory transactions per second, 120k transactions per second with full I/O, 5,600 requests per second in staging and a 99% cache-hit rate. More importantly, the same offset model defines normal processing and crash recovery.
takeaways: Serialization can be a scaling technique when the real contention is concentrated on a small number of inventory keys; removing locks and context switches may matter more than adding worker threads.
The queue offset is not only consumer metadata. It is a checkpoint that connects the transaction log, local memory and the persistent database into one recoverable state machine.
Warehouse adjustments and customer purchases share one mutation path. A unified command model removes duplicated inventory logic and makes ordering rules explicit.

Cross-service correctness is handled as a lifecycle: reserve stock, observe the order result, then confirm or compensate. Timeouts, duplicate events and reversals are part of the design rather than exceptional cases.
The architecture separates the latency-sensitive decision from durable persistence, but only because replay and idempotency make that separation safe.
review_lenses: Recovery boundary: identify exactly which offset is durable and prove that replay cannot apply an inventory mutation twice.
Hot-key strategy: decide when one processor is enough and how a SKU or warehouse could be partitioned without breaking ordering.
Backpressure: define what happens when the persistence ring buffer or MySQL falls behind the command stream.
Reservation lifecycle: make expiry, late order events, cancellation and compensation observable and idempotent.
